My feelings for this game are kinda complicated. If you want a tl;dr just read the last paragraph. If you want to know my personal thoughts as someone who 100% this game then give the rest of it a read.

This game is unfair. There are many different mechanics that you have to juggle involving the abnormalities to avoid disaster, each unique and most of the time incredibly difficult to keep track of. On top of that, there are some cases in which you end up getting abnormalities that have rules that contradict another, so you end up having to either put up with the horrible things that entitles or reset a few days to hope you get a better roll. By the way, resetting is also an integral part of the game. You'll most likely be forced to sacrifice progress to go back and grind better employees or equipment to have a fighting chance, meaning having to redo hours of work in some cases. Then after that, the game has boss fights that make trying to get through a normal day into a nightmare by instilling EVEN MORE rules.
This game is rigged against you. It will beat you up. It wont forgive you for missing even a single beat. It will get you no matter how well you think you know the game and it'll expect you to either persevere or try again for the 10th time. To be brutally honest, it's massively unbalanced and the devs know it because that's exactly what they want, while at the same time expecting you to get through it. It's stressful and infuriating 
...but, even after countless retries, over 100 hours of trial and error, and chipping away at this game on and off for over a year and only finishing it today, I can't say I hate it. Even though the devs didn't pull their punches when designing this game, they don't necessarily insult you for your failures either. It's a hard game and they know it, but they also know that with enough time and patience, they know you can win. It's reflected with the themes in the story and the dialog written; no matter how bad things are, it's still possible to get through it. That's why I like this game so much. It doesn't patronize you by making things do less damage, it doesn't make gear cost less when you lose too many employees, it doesn't do any of that. It gives you a difficult challenge and you try to conquer it. This ties incredibly well with the story too, but I'd rather not spoil anything. Personally, I don't really care too much for stories in games, but this game has so many layers and a lot of thought put into it's world that I couldn't help but get invested. The more you learn the more you realize just how deep the rabbit hole goes. There really isn't anything quite like this game.

It's honestly hit or miss. It's incredibly difficult and it doesn't get easy. The best way to gauge if you'd like it or not is by watching a video on the first few days and see if it interests you at all. Probably to like up to day 10. You might not like it and that's okay; just pass on this game, but if you DO end up liking what you see, then you'll no doubt enjoy what this game has to offer.

Lobotomy Corporation isn’t just a game - It’s a mental construct designed to break your spirit in slow, calculated increments. It presents itself with a clean interface, some snappy corporate lingo, and an intriguing promise: “Face the fear, build the future.” But what it actually delivers is a psychological meat grinder wrapped in a twisted office simulator. The further you get into it, the more you realize it’s not just challenging, it’s really personal, the amount of mental breakdowns this game causes over a stupid lost employee that takes away lots of progress and potential luck.

From the outside, Lobotomy Corporation has the look of a quirky indie game with mysterious monsters and weird SCP-like flavor. You’re the manager. You make decisions. You run a corporation. But the reality is more sinister. This isn’t about progress. It’s about control. Or more specifically, the illusion of it. You find out you're being manipulated but you just shrug it off. This game was made in the deepest pit of hell.

You don’t play Lobotomy Corporation as much as submit to it. The UI is sterile and mechanical. The music loops calmly as if nothing horrific is happening. The serenity of the interface versus the chaos it conceals is maddening. It’s a spreadsheet hell with horror lurking behind every box and dropdown menu. Every time you hear the light bells you get a shudder of terror and trauma.

But the most punishing part isn’t even the difficulty. It’s the restarts.

Restarting in Lobotomy Corporation is an emotional event. Not because you lost. failure isn’t loud or dramatic, It’s slow. Quiet. Creeping. You gradually realize that things have gone wrong beyond recovery and then you’re faced with a cold truth: you have to go back, restart it all. Yes, you have your EGO, but at what cost?

Back to the title screen. Back to watching the same conversations, the same dialogue boxes, the same menus pretending they’re offering you choice. But you know better now: your “choices” are just new paths to different types of failure. You begin again, not because you want to, but because you have no other option.

Each restart feels heavier than the last. The game doesn’t care how many hours you put in. It barely cares what you learned. It strips you of progress like it’s a punishment. Maybe that’s the real design, an experiment not in gameplay, but in endurance.

The game is opaque by design. It feeds on your curiosity. You want to know more about the abnormalities. About the facility. About that damn ai. You convince yourself that the suffering is worth it.

But eventually, something changes. You don’t look forward to progress, you fear it. You dread unlocking something new because it means more rules, more pain, more systems layered on top of the ones you still barely just learned. You move through menus like a ghost. You no longer ragequit, you just restart again.

Because that's what Lobotomy Corporation does best, it rewires your tolerance for frustration. It trains you to accept suffering as part of the process. It slowly bleeds your motivation until you’re not even playing for fun anymore. You’re playing because you have to finish this.

Restarting in Lobotomy Corporation is not a failure state, it's a ritual. A reset of your expectations. A moment to realize that what you learned doesn’t matter. This is not a game that teaches you to overcome. It teaches you to endure.

But if the constant restarting is the erosion of your will, the combat is the jagged edge that slices through whatever resolve you have left.

Combat isn’t designed to be “fun.” It’s not cinematic or reactive. You watch tiny people fight horrors not with strategy, but with hope. You assign them like a manager signing a death warrant. When agents die, they don’t scream. They brutally explode. Like data being deleted.

And maybe that’s worse.

Then there are the Abnormalities that don’t just kill you, they humiliate you. Some combat encounters aren’t about strength. They’re about absurd, almost puzzle-like mechanics. You walk into a fight only to watch half your team melt, explode, go insane, or turn on the others. All because you didn't spend 6 points to read another document.

No fight is fair. No breach is manageable unless you’ve already seen it before and memorized it. Even then, the game stacks the odds. A weak agent’s panic can trigger a chain reaction. One breach leads to another. Panic spreads. Clerks die. And all you can do is watch the spiral unfold.

Combat feels like solving a Rubik’s Cube while it’s on fire and someone’s deleting the instructions in real time. You keep trying because you think you’re learning. But sometimes the game just says “no.” Sometimes it rewards cruelty and punishes empathy.

And then, the true insanity sets in, the knowledge that even if you win the fight, you probably lost the day.

You lost your best agents. You lost valuable gear. You lost time. And in Lobotomy Corporation, time is agony. So what do you do? You reload. Or worse. You restart because you realize how bad your facility placement was too late.

And let’s not forget the Ordeals. These aren’t encounters. These are punishment rituals. They spawn in silence and erupt in chaos. The game throws them at you to see how long it takes before you break.

This isn't a power fantasy. It's a fragility simulator. A machine that shows you how little control you have, how combat isn’t the climax, it’s the cost of curiosity and the life of your Sephirah.

And you’ll fight anyway. Because a part of you wants to prove something to the game, to yourself.

But the game doesn’t care.

You fight. You lose. You restart. And the machine spins on.

At some point, you stop seeing your employees as people. Not because you want to. But because the system trains you to.

In the beginning, you care. You name your agents. You monitor their stats. You celebrate when they survive. You tell yourself you’re doing your best.

But that doesn’t last.

Eventually, someone dies. Then another. And another. And you realize. You can’t protect them all.

So your mindset shifts.

You stop naming them. They become tools. Resource vessels. A Level 5 agent with high Fortitude is a unit, not a person. You start arranging them like chess pieces. You start sacrificing them. Not with guilt, but with efficiency. You rationalize it. And you move on.

And that's exactly what the game wants from you.

Because Lobotomy Corporation isn’t just about managing a facility. It’s about surrendering to it. It invites you in with the promise of order, then reveals a system where life is just another resource. The longer you play, the more robotic you become. You send agents into death traps to test abnormalities. You use lives to gain knowledge.

And the most terrifying part? You start calling that progress.

By the midpoint of your playthrough, you’ve become the thing the game critiques. You embody the corporation. You sacrifice the weak. You repeat tragedies because the cost of learning is blood. You’re part of the machine.

The dehumanization is a psychological transformation. The game doesn’t make you into a monster. It shows you that you already were one. It just gave you a clean space to let it happen.

And if you reflect on who you've become. If you think back to the first agent you tried to protect, you might feel something.

But it won’t last. Because the next day is about to begin.

And there’s no time to feel. Only time to optimize.

Oh you have time to read? Well then, let's go a bit more in depth. First off, what even is Lob Corp?
The official page tells you it's a Monster Manager... And while it is one, that's not all it is. I'd almost see it as more Souls-like than anything. This game WILL make you suffer, whether you want it or not. Compared to many other games, Lob Corp does not help you, it does not make your journey easier. It's always bothering you, in an intended way or not.

Now, how do you play exactly? Well, it's pretty simple. The game is divided in Days, and  each Day, you will have to extract an Abnormality (or Abno, ), which will get added to your Facility. You will then have to manage this Facility, working on said Abnos to gather energy, up to a certain quota that will increase every Day, while trying not to lose every single employees in the Facility.

You know what? It'll be easier if I did the good/bad things of this game. Let's start off with...

The Good Things:
* The Lore: ohmygod the lore. If you don't wanna play Library of Ruina (the sequel) right now, you will after finishing this game.
* The Characters: it, again, doesn't actually change the game, but the character designs are just incredible.
* The Abnormalities: again, the lore is incredible, but they are also basically all different, all have different mechanics, and I swear to god at the end of this game you will not see trains the same way (trust me).
* The Game Loop: though simple, it's still pretty well executed, but it also brings a problem we'll see later...
* The Music: listen to First Trumpet or Second Trumpet, or Circle Rombed Oxygen (or not if you think it'll spoil you). Those musics man...
* The Polishing: despite what I'll say later, this game is extremely well polished. The style is well made, there are sounds for basically everything, AND THE MUSICS MAN-

But now, we got to get to...
The Bad Things (because there are some):
* Respect for Player's Time: as you can see, I played 110 hours. And I wouldn't say I'm the worst guy when playing this game, though I could have probably instead played for 140 hours if I restarted again to get the 100%. Just so you know, you will probably have to play this game basically three times to get the 100% and the secret Ending that goes with it. Also, some PARTICULAR days make you have to go very far into it, putting like 30-40 minutes, and then easily kills you and makes you restart those 40 DAMN MINUTES!!
* Aging: yeah, this game didn't age really well. And it shows with the next point...
* Bugs: there are bugs. Minor ones, like some Abno not doing exactly what it's supposed to do (I'm looking at you, Luminous Bracelet), but also pretty major ones, like the memory leak. Basically, you will have to play on a timer, because more than 1 hour on a single day will probably fill your computer's memory up and even make you crash the game (I once had my game crash three times on the same DAY WTF). There are also visual bugs (animations not triggering, VFX not despawning), and some things simply not well done (e.g. for a specific Abno, you need one of your stats to be lower than a certain amount, however that Abno will sometimes increase this Stat, and because it increases the Stat BEFORE making the check for the "is the Stat lower than X", you can be screwed because of that, yes I just ranted about a very specific thing that will probably not happen to you, I don't care).
* Difficulty Curve: though I can't tell you much right now without spoiling, you will feel the immediate increase coming out of nowhere, most of the time between Day 21 and Day 25.

However, for the last two problems, there is a solution: MODS!! The memory leak can be fixed using BaseMod I believe (right here: https://www.nexusmods.com/lobotomycorporation/mods/2), which also is the base (heh) for many other mods that fix other minor problems. You should also put mods that make the game easier, and by "make the game easier", I mean:
* More Detailed Info, which should honestly already be in the game (https://www.nexusmods.com/lobotomycorporation/mods/47)
* Free Change Appearance (https://www.nexusmods.com/lobotomycorporation/mods/39)
* Any other that seem balanced, because though it's cool to want to finish the game without mods, it's even cooler to ACTUALLY FINISH IT. I didn't use any mods, and I HAD to take a 1-2 months break from the game to come back better. That is how hard and frustrating this game is.

If you've read all of this well done. If you still won't buy this game, uh, good for you. You won't have to endure the pain.

If you did however... Prepare. Oh, and...

Welcome to Lobotomy Corporation, Manager.

This game hates you.

No, really. It hates you. It hates your guts, it hates your attempts, it will chew you up because you decided to take in a new Abnormality (Totally Not SCP), send one of your agents in, and 30 seconds later, wonder why it mutated into a middle-tier slime that's currently infecting others and cascading into your 5th reset of the hour.

And when the hooks are in deep enough? You shrug it off. You reset. You start seeing your agents as disposable beings that are just there to survive until the next bit. You get to the next day with 3 dead. This is a good thing. 3 dead is easily replaceable. Dead people are replacable.

You watch someone grow for 10 days. Level 4. Researching the higher tier monsters. You screw up. You see them immediately die because the roulette hated them enough that they were chosen for a sacrifice to an Abnormality that hits way above your paygrade. You wonder if you can save them. You decide not to. You hit a wall. No matter what, this next part is impossible. Reset upon reset. A Memory Imprint a few days back; something's stopping, you're not lucky enough the list goes on.

That's fine. Day 1 reset. You keep the knowledge of the Abnormalities you researched. Certain meta tidbits are preserved. You go again. Try a few new ones. Fall back on the ones that you know won't screw you over. Repeat. And again. 

The game is jank. The game has questionable elements. The game has a few Missing Staircase things and Abnormalities that deliberately kick you in the nuts while you're down. The game's translation could stand to have stronger character voices, a clearer emphasis on how you're supposed to take this game, a combat system micro that isn't so finicky, on and on and on. It's the product of a failed kickstarter that somehow made it to the light of day in all its flawed glory.

And it works. The brainworms hit me. Even when every later day ended with a sense of dread at what's coming next, what the plot wishes to give, what the characters want to do, even when it'd be better to close it and relax...The agents get prepped. The Abnormalities are extracted. And the days go on.

What it gets right is the feeling. It has an atmosphere in mind, something intertwining directly back to the setting, the plot, the reason you're in L Corp in the first place, doing all this while an AI directs you again and again and again. It's the ludonarrative aspect that's the true king here, and your enjoyment of this is entirely predicated on understanding what the game wants you to feel and how much you buy into it. The gameplay and stress work so well with the plot that leaving it out for a plot video is a disservice. 

It's hard to emphasize how much this game gets right in terms of gameplay and plot working together without spoiling stuff. The barest knowledge is that you're there for a reason. There's a reason why the protagonist doesn't up and quit.

If it's too hard, mod it. Zero shame. The game is tough as nails. Get stuff from Nexus Mods. Super Agents (It will not save you). Infinite Points. Learn when your own wellbeing is better than cracking against this wall of a game and break it down with the mods to experience the gameplay interplay with the story at hand. The mods will not make this a 100% cakewalk, but it'll lessen some of the more demanding aspects...and not all of it.

Lobotomy Corporation seeks out to rekindle the magical horror and wonderment of classic SCP (you know, when SCP was any good) with a shocking degree of success. It's an intriguing, imaginative, engrossing and wonderfully engaging experience, while also being extremely bleak, horrific and best/worst of all, overwhelmingly painful and genuinely sadistically cruel.

This is a remarkably charming management game, with a striking artstyle, creative creature designs, and compelling characters with a subtle, yet very notable line of dark humor sprinkled throughout. 
The story and setting are by far the biggest hook, keeping you engaged as you progress days of work. All of the cast members are at a bare minimum interesting to learn more about, and their contrasting personalities play off well with the bleakness of the situations you will encounter. 
If anything, and this will make sense later, the overarching plot and wanting to know more about the titular Corporation and who these people are will most likely be the determining factor of whenever or not you want to beat the game.

The first 2/3's of the game have what I would call a punishing yet overall "fair" challenge. 

You lose some blokes, you experiment, you maximize performance and learn the ins-and-out of each anomaly to produce the most energy to finish a day. 
You beat some missions for valuable upgrades and progress in the development of your equipment. 
You fail miserably and start again, with more experience and confidence. Now you know what to avoid, you feel the progress you've made, and can ease yourself out of situations that got you a game over before, or avoid them entirely.

And for the grand majority of the game, it just works. The game is absolutely ruthless, but for the most part, once you know what’s the rhythm and what the monsters do, mistakes and losses are truly felt as your own. There is a genuine satisfaction in managing to achieve victories out of such desperate, grim and completely FUBAR scenarios.

Because when the alerts go off, Lobotomy Corporation manages to be one of the finest “Oooooh shit” simulators on the market. Making calls becomes a true life or death scenario, as losing staff actually hurts given the investments to level them up. As chaos erupts, it becomes a bigger and bigger disaster to even hope to manage. 
The game shines when the music kicks into total overdrive, shifting the tense yet strangely cozy ambience of the facility into a every-man-for-himself clusterfuck of screaming, gibs, and pure horror.

It's the final set of days that makes this game such a difficult recommendation. 

Your facility can easily become a flat out unwinnable Rube Goldberg machine which at the first mistake (or even none at all) will spell a domino effect ending in a total disaster. And by this point you can only start over, wasting hours of playtime from scratch. Even when you know everything the game can throw at you, it's still possible to fail miserably without a chance to recover, and some abnormality combinations that can happen by the cruel hand of RNG can make your life a living hell. And when you have no choice but to do so much over again, it’s extremely easy to simply lose all the goodwill towards the game. 
The late game unlocks do help alleviate some of the frustrations when having to do-over, but they also provide incredible levels of suffering to unlock, and are also extremely difficult under most conditions.
In a personal griviance, I only play on a Steam Deck these days because I no longer have a PC, and the visual effects and filters in some endgame portions are essentially eye-strain torture.

Aside from all that, there are multiple severe game breaking bugs and optimization issues involving a memory leak, most notably one of the unlockable perks (which I consider straight up essential in some scenarios) is completely broken and does not work. I know the answer is obviously "just use mods", but a game should not require mods for an essential feature to function in my opinion, or to avoid memory leaks by endgame. And given the fact Project Moon is still an active developer making sweet gacha money, I see no reason why they couldn't simply insert the fan-made fixes into the game, at least the optimization mod and the unlockable fix.

Overall, I cannot in good conscience recommend Lobotomy Corporation to practically 95% of the human population, even if I have to give credit for having such a well thought out narrative with a genuinely amazing ensamble of characters, a cool setting with cool monsters, and for keeping the spirit of old school SCP alive with an excellent execution.

It all really comes down to the final haul being such a brutal difficulty spike, and the severe game breaking issues that are holding it back for me to be able to encourage most people to give this game a try.

It's a game that you essentially have to force yourself to see the bitter end, kicking and screaming in agony across the finish line, dragged in a hedge of nails, and you do it purely out of spite or because you just wanna see for yourself what happens next in the story. 
Only completely deranged masochists would sincerely enjoy everything the game has to offer, and I believe that while the good outweighs the bad, the bad simply profoundly affects the experience to the point I cannot encourage playing this game to basically anyone but those with a superlative endurance and patience.

Lobotomy Corporation is simultaneously a creepy game, a relaxing game, and an intense game, with an intriguing world and criminally low sales. You definitely should buy it if your dream is to manage an occult research facility, while facing fears and overlooking casualties. 

You can call this game a “nightmare research manager”: it’s all about researching scary unspeakable things, entertaining scary unspeakable things to keep them inside their chambers, and harvesting energy from scary unspeakable things, all to get through another day. I have a lot of respect for the people who made this game, and I'll more than happily play their other products, but I just had too many problems build up as I went through the game, but incase you do get the game my best advice to give would be this.

Don't be afraid of replaying/restarting, even from Day 1.
The games expects you to use memory repository, and the only thing you will lose from going back, even to day 1, are the employees that you hired, and the abnormalities you obtained.
However any items and/or information you obtained from those abnormalities is kept.
Mission progress/completion is also kept, even from Day 1 resets, this makes replaying the game significantly easier, so do not be afraid of this, or losing employees.

With that said, I actually have a fair amount of nice things to say about the game, so let's start off with the

+++Positives+++

The thematics of the game are great!
I thought the general aesthetic worked really well, both for budget reasons and as an intentional style.
But beyond graphics, there's a lot of horror vibes, the store description doesn't lie with what it's inspired by, I really liked the SCP vibes throughout.

Speaking of SCP's, the Abnormalities are numerous and varied, I loved how different a lot of them were, and it was surprisingly satisfying figuring out how to manage them all and in the end, profit off them.

The story was also pretty neat, though I can't go into depth about it.
I found my eyes glazing over it a smidge with how it was worded at points, but overall I liked how dark it was throughout and how things played out with all of the characters.

Lastly, the music was also pretty cool at points.
For the most part it was kinda samey unless things were going wrong, but when things WERE going wrong, it got pretty good.

Now onto the 

---Negatives---

The games performance is terrible, specifically as you progress.
What started out perfectly smooth devolved into low framerates as the facility expanded, to the point where even loading screens came close to crashing the game if I clicked or alt tabbed.
This is a problem when you're faced with combat, because when particle effects happen, the game practically freezes momentarily, but everything is combat has particle effects.
Damage prompts, insanity prompts, blood splatters, everything will cause lag if you use large groups.
Now while small groups have their benefits, being discouraged from using a large group because the games performance will just die along with all my lower level employees, feels terrible.
But even outside of combat, scrolling across the facility is laggy, animations get less smooth and for the late game objectives specifically, it just feels awful.

To go more in-depth on combat, it's really simple. You select employees and you can tell them to either go to a location, or attack something, and later on in the game you get bullets, which let you manually target people to give them shields, health, sanity or just kill them if they start to become troublesome.
But my problem with combat is that it's too simple, I cannot tell an employee where specifically I want them in a room, I can only tell them I want them in that room. So when I'm fighting an enemy and I want to move them to the other side of said enemy, I have to select the employee, tell them to go into a room on the other side of the enemy (assuming there even is one, otherwise their only option is to either get hit or leave the room entirely), wait for the employee to move, select them again and tell them to attack the enemy.
It's tedious, it's clunky and it's one of the reasons I disliked when the game decided to delve more into combat specifically.

Speaking of those objectives from earlier, throughout the entire game you're given missions from different people in the facility, culminating in a final objective from them. These started off perfectly fine, but the last few in particular were just awful.
I will spoil three of these in particular but these are not major plot spoilers, just gameplay ones.
[spoiler]Starting with the Disciplinary Team, I don't understand why they had boss fights be the days objective instead of just collecting energy, the game is not built for boss fights as it just devolves into kiting attacks over and over, even with your best units. But for your units which aren't the best, you just kinda have them on the side, lest they die and ruin everyone elses sanity.
It's a boring fight which you cheese either via kiting, or through some other method, such as unleashing Abnormalities to the work for you, which sounds like a smart use of mechanics but it's pretty dull [/spoiler]

[spoiler]Next is the Record Team, this one is just dull. It takes away your ability to pause and manage things (to an extent), but it also removes your ability to speed things up, opting to speed things up gradually as the day goes along. I find this extremely boring, as most abnormalities don't use time as a mechanic, so it just makes the day go extremely slowly, and if you need to restart, you'll feel every second crawl on by. [/spoiler]

[spoiler]Finally we have the Extraction Team, another mission that requires you to finish a boss fight instead of getting enough energy, so what this means is more kiting to avoid attacks. The gimmick with this boss is cool, you cannot hurt the boss until you deal with specific Abnormalities that get put into a meltdown state.
Once they're vulnerable, you have a good chunk of time to wail on them. There are several problems here. She can place her meltdown effect on abnormalities which are already on cooldown, meaning you need to wait unnecessarily before you can send someone to deal with it, and when the boss becomes vulnerable, they stop for a long while, even if they're in a doorway transition where you cannot reach their model. If you do not deal with them in this state, there is a good chance they'll throw out more meltdowns again, all because you literally could not reach them because the game didn't allow you to.[/spoiler]

And going back to general gameplay, I really wish the game had more automation.
A lot of days, I was just going through the motions, it would've been nice if there was some way I could just automatically send people to go do the jobs I would like them to do. Replaying days felt boring, because very little changed, and as the facility expanded, the fatigue really set in.

And speaking of the facility, I mentioned how I loved the variety of abnormalities earlier, but sometimes the game can give you some abnormalities you're just not able to deal with at points.
Some will get out because you have too many clerk casualties, one will get out because you don't have enough clerk casualties, some will get out because your employees are too underleveled or undergeared and in the worst case scenario, you're getting them on days where a checkpoint is set and going back to said checkpoint fixes nothing. Going back isn't bad, but the reason for it can definitely feel bad.

>>Conclusion<<
Overall, there was a lot I like about the game, and it started off real strong, but it just became so tedious and annoying with what I wanted from me later on.
It's not devoid of quality, and it definitely appeals to some people, but I find that it was more annoying than anything else in the later game for me to recommend this personally.

At 279 hours I have officially completed the game in its entirety.

Is this game hard? Yes. It is a game about trying, essentially, to trip up the player. It's a rube-goldberg machine of carefully calculated dick moves. There's an evergrowing list of rules with each abnormality you get: some very simple, others frustratingly complicated, but there is a list for each. For any rule, there is an abnormality with the exact opposite rule: some will punish you on Bad results, others on Bad or Neutral. Some will punish you on [i]only[/i] Neutral, some on Good or Bad results. The game will generously keep track of these rules as you discover them, but you are drawn endlessly into the web. You will get comfortable with these rules in time, but just as you get comfortable the game will begin to alter the deal, and your prayers that it not be altered further will fall on deaf ears. "Is it hard?" You know in being a Korean game it reminds me a lot of Starcraft and the Korean fascination with that: Starcraft is desperately hard, but if you know what to do, and can perfectly execute it, it's easy. If you can't, well, you'll endure. Restarting and Resetting are major game mechanics without which the game cannot actually be completed (literally it is not possible to complete the game in one run without at least one memory reset).

Is it interesting? [i]Desperately.[/i] The story told by Lobotomy Corporation is one I very much enjoy and one that draws you, the player, in as the participate. There aren't choices to make though; rather, the only choices are the ones you come up with to meet the challenges. For the game weaves the story and the difficulty together, as you, the Manager of this strange facility, desperately try to comprehend what it is that you are doing here and why.

You will come to love your agents, you will suit them up in a variety of colorful equipment, and you will send them to their horrible deaths over and over and over. Decapitated, eaten alive, flattened like a pancake, ripping off their own head, dragged to hell, digested by spiders, turned *into* an interdimensional spider, turning into a giant mushroom, turned into a small slime, turned into a large slime, vaporized, pulverized, incinerated, frozen, ground into meat chunks, killed by their fellow agents after they lost their minds and had to be put down, executed with impunity by the manager... and this is not even nearly close to the many deaths you will see them suffer. You will reset and do it again. The charmingly horrible deaths are a balm of sorts: I remember a desperately frustrating death, but watching the individual in question lower themselves into a bath full of blood and grimly deciding I needed to keep going with the day is part of the experience.

This game can be clunky, it's not exceptionally polished, there are infrequent graphical glitches and a few bugs that I had to go and install mods for (it's not necessary to do so, but I wanted to). This game will not be an easy experience, but if you are willing to Face the Fear, and Build the Future, you will enjoy it. I think that this game is [u]unrelenting[/u], and absolutely uncompromising, but slowly bending it to your will until you stand at the end over a pile of corpses and regrets in bloody triumph is one hell of an experience and one I am so glad I decided to play.

[b]Overview[/b]

Pros :
- The only SCP-like management game that you'll ever find
- Story rich game in a cyberpunk dystopian setting with fantasy elements
- Roleplaying elements
- Unique monster mechanics and interesting lores
- The game will throw surprises at you
- Character customization for employees
- Hard game

Cons :
- UI is a little bit clunky
- FPS drops sometimes
- Gameplay can be a bit repetitive
- Training employees can be grindy
- Hard game

[b]Full Review[/b]

Lobotomy Corporation is a monster management game where you manage creatures called Abnormalities in a very SCP like fashion. You play as a manager overseeing Abnormalities by assigning your employees to work on the Abnormalities. Each of the Abnormalities has its own set of rules to determine how to best deal with it. These rules are hidden at first, so you must do a little experimentation before you can unlock them.

Each day that you complete a level, you have to pick one of three Abnormalities that are offered. As you progress more, the threat level for Abnormalities that you encounter will increase. You will also discover that not only you have to manage these Abnormalities on their own, some of them can also interact with other Abnormality. This is what I will call a "combo". Some combos can be helpful to you, but a lot of them are really deadly. This is where most of the difficulty comes in. 

As I mentioned earlier, the game can be really brutal and if you find yourself stuck on a day or level because you can't manage these Abnormalities, it will be better to use a feature called "Memory Repository" to go back in time. It will allow you to repick Abnormalities. Worst case scenario, you will have to reset to day 1, but don't worry as you will keep your Abnormalities informations and equipments. You will also find yourself progress the day a lot more quicker than before. The negative is the game can become a bit repetitive after a while, especially after you unlocked a lot of the informations and equipments, but the game will throw surprises at you and it was enough to keep me interested.

As for the story, I personally really like it. Without spoiling anything, the story takes place in a cyberpunk dystopian setting with a lot of fantasy elements thrown in, which I don't see that many of. It is presented in a style that is similar to a visual novel. This game also has a sequel called "Library of Ruina", so if you are interested in the story and world of Lobotomy Corporation, you might want to check that game out as well.

When these two meet, Little Red is almost certainly going to win the matchup, and will return to her containment automatically, her bloodlust sated, as long as she is the one to land the killing blow on That Bitch Wolf. The gameplay is fairly simple to grasp. You have an Abnormality who is sitting in a nice little Containment Cell. You have an Agent who needs to gather energy from it. You chose what type of work to perform, and that's it. You watch the little guy go and hope for the best. If you're a good manager, this game will become routine, almost tedious in its design. If everything is performing as intended, all you do is schedule your little guys to do their little works and once you've got enough energy you move on to the next day to continue the story. But not everything goes as you want it to.

Every single Abnormality has its own list of rules that must be obeyed. This Abnormality kills you if your work time takes too long. This one gives you a gift, but if you work on another Abnormality while carrying its gift you die and turn into a horrible monster. This one doesn't like Repression work. That one hates employees with high Temperance. These are all rules you'll have to tuck away into your subconscious as you play the game. Forget any one rule, and you're likely to have an employee die. I once had spent a few hours on a single day trying to grind my employee's stats to maximum for upcoming challenges. I had one employee work with a safe abnormality who gives a little healing orb for doing work. It's not an abnormality that's good at training stats however, so I sent that employee to work with another to finish off her stats. To my dismay I forgot that anyone carrying the orb is likely to die if they work on any other Abnormality. Not only that, but any employees who got the orb throughout the day ALSO die when that happens, causing 5 deaths in my facility of 20 employees.

But this is where the game really starts to shine in my opinion. You can Retry at almost any time. Those 5 employees are back under my care, as though nothing had ever happened. I was a bit aggravated to lose my employees, but it was my fault. Fundamentally, Lobotomy Corp does not present the player with impossible tasks. There is never a case where an employees death is a requirement to progress. Some challenges can be made easier by throwing a few corpses at it. One of the hardest challenges in the entire game can be made trivial if you're willing to commit to sacrificing a single employee, but it's never a requirement to progress. A deathless run is more than doable. Everything comes down to player knowledge. In that way this game is a little bit like Outer Wilds. Your own knowledge is one of the strongest weapons at your disposal.

But then it gets even better. Every 5 days the game saves to something called the Memory Repository. Any gear you've unlocked, quests completed, research gained, and upgrades acquired persist when returning to the Memory Repository. That one sacrifice to cheese one of the hardest encounters in the game? That employee too can come back. The challenge will still be cleared. And you will have new resources available further challenges even easier. You can go through a week, farm a bunch of high level gear, and return to the start of the week with everyone alive and now decked out in the high level gear you just earned.

And so eventually we return to the status quo. My entire facility is now flooded with Level V Agents with maxed out stats and EGO Gifts. My facility is so powerful we can set dangerous ALEPH class Abnormalities free for fun and easily suppress them without a single lost employee. And so the game has returned to that tedium I mentioned before. If you're a good manager, nothing will go wrong. If nothing is going wrong, then all you're really doing is farming energy and moving along. The game has two ways of co this fatigue. Ordeals, and Missions.

Missions are challenges set forth by the other characters in the game. Most of these are pretty easy, but some can be quite challenging. One of them is Suppress 3 different ALEPH Class Abnormalities in a single day. For someone like me with a small army of super units decked out in the best gear thanks to judicious use of time travel, this is fairly trivial. But for most players this is a wall that will be nearly insurmountable. They also reward you with permanent upgrades.

The second mechanic is Ordeals. These are essentially uncontained Abnormalities that appear randomly throughout the day. The game gives you a warning before they spawn, and the player themselves must trigger the event by performing work. The first time you encounter an Ordeal it will likely be a nightmare. You won't understand what these clowns are. you won't be in position to stop them, and you won't understand why Der Freishutz just shot a bullet down a hallway and killed half your employees. Eventually you'll learn that the clowns spawn in random hallways, but only one per department. You'll learn that their goal is to either breach or trigger the special ability of an abnormality in their hallway, and you'll learn that you can easily hard counter them by placing one employee per hallway ahead of time. And that's only  Crimson Dawn, one of the easiest Ordeals to handle. Thankfully though every single Ordeal save one is just like this. They have a very obvious counterplay, and once you understand it you won't lose an Employee to it ever again. Except for Violet Midnight. If you see Violet Midnight just hit that Retry button I guess. It ain't worth it.

And thus we once again return to the norm. You've completed the missions, you know how to handle Ordeals, your abnormalities are safe. And then the game starts throwing something else at you that pushes you to the brink. Suddenly you get a challenge where all your work Orders are scrambled. Your employee stats are lowered. Healing is disabled. A skilled player will not be used to putting out fires. They'll prevent the fires from happening in the first place through diligent management. And then the game sets off an inferno, and tells you "Adapt or die." These are some of the most fun challenges the game has to offer, but also the most difficult. These moments are stressful, tense, and you'll probably have to retry some of them several times before you clear the challenge, but at the same time the catharsis once you do is one of the best. And remember, all of the above is still in play during these challenges. Abnormalities still need work.

I could honestly say as much about the story as I've said about the gameplay. I found the characters endearing and charming. The abnormalities are as much a character as anything else in this game, and most of them are lovely. My personal favorite is probably CENSORED. An abnormality that pokes fun at all those childishly written SCP Articles where they try to add mystique and danger by just spamming [REDACTED] all over the page. The abnormality itself is a giant censor bar because it's so horrifying to look at that even you, the manager, would die just seeing it. Top class stuff. Despite its arguably horror roots and shocking, violent content, the game isn't afraid to be a bit cheeky and playful with it all. The game's setting is one that will sneak up on you. The true nature of the City, and the world they all live in is fairly compelling anti-capitalist stuff. One of my favorite Abnormalities is a blind birth with a crooked Scales of Justice hanging on its neck. The bird cannot tell that the scales are crooked because it is blind. Absolutely flawless symbolism.

The music is also great. There's only like 10 tracks total, but they're all wonderful and never get grating despite looping constantly. The graphics are clumsy, and the game is a bit poorly programmed and janky in spots, but everything else fantastic.

TLDR: Lobotomy Corporation is a tough, but ultimately fair game with lots of replay value wrapped in a great story with sometimes tedious gameplay. Surprisingly well balanced in spite of what others have said about vertical difficulty spikes or impossible challenges. 9/10, I could have gone on, but I ran out of space. Oops.

Lobotomy Corporation, despite it being one of my favorite works of media in terms of story and setting, is a mixed bag in term of an overall game. It's something that isn't for everyone, but something I would nonetheless recommend to those who might fit it (hell, I've written lengthy fanfictions regarding it, so that's something to note).

[b] The Good: [/b] The experience of working with strange creatures and slowly discovering how to use them and work around them feels wonderfully evocative of SCP Foundation-like stories; this is a game you REALLY, REALLY want to go into unspoiled. 

The character designs are nice, the music despite mostly being not made for the game is incredibly well chosen, and most of all; the story and setting designs have so much thought clearly put into them that it feels like an incredibly well plotted out dystopian setting, a fact that I'm sure the seuqel Library of Ruina will only flesh out more when it's released.

[b] The Bad: [/b] The gameplay, while fun at first, can become repetitive later; especially when you're managing several Abnormalities you're used to and going through days that can take upwards of 15 minutes at times, and ESPECIALLY if you're restarting a day repeatedly for a specific option or trying to deal with a specific boss battle. It can get grindy, so be prepared for that.
It's also quite difficult at points, and will often require you to rewind and try things again if you fucked up too many times or didn't do well enough. If you give up easily, this game probably isn't for you!

[b] The Elephant in the Room: [/b] A notable fact, and a fact that will likely be remedied soon, is that for several years this game has had an infamously bad translation as a result of the dev team being essentially scammed. However, a retranslation by a dedicated fan group that'll be added officially to the game is in the works to fix this. Despite that, for the best experience, I'd personally recommend waiting until the translation is complete to play the game - the lore in this thing is T H I C C, and you'd be really cheating yourself by experiencing it through an indecipherable and confusing lens.

Lobotomy Corporation is a management style game with an infamous reputation for being extremely difficult and unforgiving to the point of not really being "fun" anymore, in a similar vein to Pathologic and other such experiences. At first I felt the same way, but after trying the game again I've come to the conclusion that this view is shortsighted, but its still partially the games fault. In short, Lobotomy Corp is a difficult game that DEMANDS that you learn its systems to survive, but patently encourages learning and exploration rather than being the untowardly punishing experience it is known for. Its still hard, but they expect you to struggle rather than punish you for struggling. Difficulty might be what it's known for, but Lobo Corp won't kick you while you're down. If you can offer the patience to deal with its eccentricities, I highly recommend Lobotomy Corp.

GAMEPLAY: The basic gameplay loop of Lobotomy Corp involves selecting an abnormality most days (essentially an SCP), then reaching an energy quota to pass the day by interacting with said abnormalities through various means. Every aspect of this is dangerous, and its your job to manage your employees safely. This includes how/when/why they work with abnormalities, preventing abnormalities from escaping, equipping and managing gear acquired by working with abnormalities (called EGO), and building up various departments in the company by progressing and completing missions each day. Mostly this comes down to limiting the amount of [i]untimely doom[/i] experienced by your employees. As the game progresses you gain more and more control over how this is done, including some buffs/heals/other ways of directly helping out.

However, a lot of what you can and can't do isn't immediately obvious. Rather than unlocking bonuses, your most prominent strengths largely come from understanding. In my opinion learning the game is the truest experience of the game itself, so by discussing these I'll be taking something away from the gameplay itself so consider yourself warned. Spoilers end at the section marked STORY.

For example, it isn't immediately obvious that you can micro groups of employees out of attacks with careful orders, or pull individuals out of danger the same way. Stacking a legion of employees into an elevator and making abnormalities "face check" it is an extremely easy way to combat many threats. You're not forced to end a day when your quota is complete, so you can stay and power level employees if you can take the heat from doing so. Learning to balance the damage types of weapons within a department, how to equip high/low level employees, how to use various abnormalities to your own benefit, etc, I could go on. All of these are available from the second the game starts, but even thinking to try them will probably take some time.

Another option available immediately is not one, not two, but three different resets to roll back time. One resets the day (after you pick an abnormality but before the day starts,) one resets the week (including subsequently picked abnormalities, we'll come back to that,) and one resets all the way to day 1. You're probably thinking why on earth would I ever want that, can I softlock myself or something? While its definitely possible to get so far in the hole or stuck with abnormalities you can't handle, that isn't the only reason. You see the only "true" reset is the day reset. The Week and Day 1 reset both keep most of your hard work intact, including abnormality information and EGO. Gathering abnormality info is the single most dangerous activity in Lobotomy Corp, so if you get something you absolutely can't handle why not just research it then bail? Furthermore, every time you pick an abnormality its essentially done mostly blind UNLESS you have their info already so you'll know exactly what you're getting into if you ever reset and come across it again. Even if you struggle constantly and fail miserably, most of the hard work you've done is kept if you restart. As another example of hidden tactics, nothing is stopping you from gathering all the info on a new abnormality at the start of the day (at the cost of employee mortality) and just writing it down and immediately reseting to do it right. Its not an exploit, its intended.

Here lies Lobotomy Corps greatest strength, but also its greatest weakness in my opinion. By trusting you to figure all this out on your own, it runs the risk of many players simply bouncing off it. This style of design is likely responsible for both its cult following AND its infamous reputation. See, what I didn't mention is the exact details of these resets are never clearly explained to you AFAIK. Additionally, many negative reviews mention the lack of speed up, employee health on the UI, and other features. But the kicker is you DO get these features... a little while into the game. Many people are repulsed an hour in and give up, and I can't really blame them in good conscience. If you were willing to invest the time and effort (and risk) to learn this on your own its no problem, but [strike]without being a wiki warrior[/strike] I'd wager 90% of people would be afraid to dive in like that. What sucks is diving in headlong really is the best way to play, and there are numerous safety nets to enable this, but [i]you won't know they're there[/i] until you experience them. Once all the systems click, its really not that hard. There are so many tricks you can use to get ahead, and once you start to "get it" it feels great.

STORY: I'm not going to discuss the story of Lobotomy Corp explicitly. However, I want to emphasize how good the flavor of the setting Project Moon has created is, as well as it being perfectly logically consistent between all three games (Lobotomy Corporation, Library of Ruina, Limbus Company.) In short, its one of the most interesting dystopias I've ever seen. Human life has little value, but unlike many similar settings its inhabitants are well aware of how awful things are and no one is happy about it. It's weirdly [i]not[/i] hopeless, and all three games feature consistent themes of trying to find improvement and meaning. Suffice to say its very, very good. The 3 games are DIRECT SEQUALS to each other, so if you like one you'll almost certainly like the others.

CONCLUSION: My biggest take away is that if everyone who played Lobotomy Corp was forced to see it through during a prison sentence or something, I think the perception of the game would be far less negative. However, that's still asking quite a lot. At its core, Lobotomy corp trusts the player a LOT, maybe even too much. Trusts you to keep pushing on your own to figure things out and find solutions unprompted. For some this will be very refreshing, but others won't want to deal with it. Its almost a case study of game design, the kind of thing you can only ever love or hate. That being said, I highly recommend it.

Lobotomy Corporation is a management game in which you must send your employees to work with "abnormalities", which can be not just monsters, but also strange beings, objects or even phenomena. Working with them generates energy, and your goal is to meet a daily energy quota to finish a day and advance to the next.

The game's strongest aspect is its very unique atmosphere. There's a very wide variety of bizarre entities, ranging all the way from the weird and funny to the incomprehensible and nightmarish, each one with its own lore that you gradually unlock as you work with them. The game has a very mysterious and ominous vibe to it, and an intriguing story that'll always keep you wondering what's next. On top of that, the soundtrack is also great; there aren't many songs overall, but those that the game does have are quite memorable and fit the dark, bizarre atmosphere very well.

Each abnormality is unique and has its own set of guidelines that you'll slowly uncover as you work with it, and you'll learn the most effective ways to deal with each abormality, and how to avoid your employees dying a horrible (perma)death when working with them. However, the game lets you retry each day as many times as you want, so you have an infinite supply of time to figure things out and master the game.

As you work with abnormalities, you also unlock extra equipment for your employees: first there's armor that not just helps protect them when an abnormality breaches and must be suppressed, but it also protects them during the work itself, as the simple act of working with an abnormality already deals damage. Second, there are weapons that help you suppress breaching abnormalities and other enemies that occasionally appear. Third, there are "gifts", little items that give each employee a small bonus in certain stats. Therefore, the game encourages you to work with all abnormalities and unlock all equipment associated with them. However, you need to be careful, because, If an employee dies, you lose their equipment and must get it again.

Due to its high difficulty, the game has some systems that help you grow stronger and more prepared for the endgame. Namely, if you restart the story mode, you actually keep all the equipment you got, and also all the information you've gathered on abnormalities, as well as any general upgrades you've unlocked. Therefore, it's a good idea to occasionally restart the game because you'll be stronger each time, and it never feels like grinding, because there are so many different abnormalities to discover, and it's impossible to see all of them in a single run. So every new restart feels fresh and fun, especially as you become more experienced and manage to beat the first few days more easily.

All in all, Lobotomy Corporation is a very unique game with an amazing atmosphere and engaging gameplay, and it presents you with a tough but fun and rewarding challenge. It'll pull you into its bizarre, intriguing world and keep you coming back to learn more and master it.

To play Lobotomy Corporation is to walk blindfolded through a minefield.  If that appeals to you, then ignore the rest of my review and buy the game right now.  You'll love it.

If you're still reading, then what's in store for you is to have your legs blown off over and over by threats you cannot foresee, cannot avoid, and very probably, will force you to reset your runs at the drop of a hat.  And it is by design.

That is, unless you cheat.  You can look up the Abnormalities (monsters) on the Wiki page, revealing all of their information with zero in-game effort.  Then, you can save scum to restart the current day, apply the perfect solution to beat them, and carry on unimpeded.  You can walk through the minefield without a scratch.  No skill, no talent, just blithely applying someone else's information in order to win.

This approach removes all of the frustration, but it also removes all of the fun.  If you know all the solutions without having to work for them, then why are you even playing in the first place?  What fun is a game about mysterious monsters, when the monsters are no longer mysterious?  By design, the game is equal parts maddening frustration and captivating horror.  If you remove the frustration, the horror stops being captivating.  You either swallow the pill whole, or not at all.

10 hours in, and this reality has finally sunk in for me.  I've been liberally reloading and reading Wiki pages so far, and I'm breezing through the game.  Until I hit the Singing Machine.  Even armed with the Wiki page, it kept killing my guys over and over.  I kept reloading and re-reading.  I thought the game was bugged at first, until I realized I was reading the rules wrong, and figured out how to overcome it. My biggest beef with Lobotomy Corporation is that it's a game that's based on knowledge, and not on skill.  You can't infer the stats or approach of a new abnormality based on past work with other creatures.

I quit at 30 hours, because the thought of putting in another 50, 100, 150 hours or whatever of stabbing in the dark and resetting days over and over after repeated failures didn't seem fun.  I hated the Singing Machine.  I hated the Woodsman.  How many more obtuse and punishing guessing games would I need to play to finish the game? Look I totally get why other people recommend the game.  It's a very intriguing and stylish guessing game.  But I don't like guessing games.

This game is good. Quality. It's not a legendary product, but it's enough for most people. However, what really carried me (and probably most people) forward was the amazing story. It's seriously well written, and such quality is taken over in the sequel Library of Ruina.

Oh yea, did I mention this game has a sequel? If you wanna see what they made from the funds of this game, go look at that game.
Anyways, regarding the gameplay- you take over as a Manager of L Corp, also known as Lobotomy Corporation. Your company is in charge of generating power in a very clean way- by interacting with special creatures known as abnormalities and making them happy. This happy energy they produce is then used to keep the city alive with power. The only problem is; most if not all abnormalities enjoy munching on your employees, splattering your clerks into paste, or just enjoy seeing your entire facility fall into ruin. I fully, 100% recommend playing this game with as little to no knowledge about the abnormalities as possible. The game shines best when you're playing it blind and are stumbling through the darkness.

The gameplay itself is fine. Initially, it's easy, but once you reach mid to late game, the difficulty starts rising sharply, showing itself as a well made management sim (especially if you picked the needy abnormalities). There are a few bugs here and there, but overall it works well. Just be warned though, endgame (the final 4 days) have a MASSIVE difficulty spike, and the game encourages you to reset until you make the game easier and easier to deal with. And by reset, I don't mean the day or the past five days, I mean back to square one. I understand that can be a turn off for some people, so I thought I'd say as much.

Music is all right, nothing too special besides the ones used for cutscenes and the last day. I recommend listening to Library of Ruina music to see what they're capable of in the future.

Visually, it's simplistic. 

Storywise, it's absolutely amazing, and you'll find there is a justification for damn near everything in the game. There are a few hints about it strewn inside abnormality lore as well, so it's really cleverly made.

All in all, I recommend this game. I'm not a fan of management games, but this one caught my attention.
8/10, would recommend beating the game just to play Library of Ruina, which is a masterpiece. (Of course, the story also makes sense for those who haven't beaten lobotomy corp, but it helps you appreciate it more).

This game and I have a funky relationship. The exploratory components of the gameplay, the writing, the music, it is all absolutely stellar. There is so much to rave about it. The thing which irks me the most about this game, however, is probably the user-hostile experience. I have not had such a user-hostile experience playing a video game before. Insufficient tutorial aside, there are a lot of weird aspects to the game which seem needlessly punishing. For example, E.G.O. loss upon employee death is quite brutal on your second+ playthrough, and it adds a needless amount of risk to giving out your most powerful E.G.O. to employees when the criteria for equipping high-level E.G.O. is already so high. In addition, the consequences of Return to Memory Repository are quite hard to read into at first. While employees who died after Memory Imprint come back to life, E.G.O. is still lost.

The most punishing aspect of the game is easily the grindy aspect. To end most days, you need to reach a certain power output level, and this makes replays incredibly tedious. What's more, without spoiling, some special days instead require you to play through days up to a certain point. Some of these days get incredibly long, and having someone in your team die with good weaponry/armor during the end of one of these long days is incredibly brutal and demoralizing.

Some of the abnormalities seem to be implemented specifically to make you vigilant (or suffer) as opposed to giving you a fun time. Of course, I can't get into these without spoiling the game, but some abnormalities are incredibly high-maintenance, high-risk for sometimes little to no reward. The only reason I managed to play this game well was because I had watched streams beforehand and knew about some of the worst abnormalities and how to deal with them as minimally as possible.

There is a modding community for this game, and near the end of my playthrough I had to download a few mods because the gameplay was becoming exceedingly, disproportionately punishing. I would heavily recommend downloading mods for this game because it is, to be frank, unfair. There is one abnormality which, if you encounter it on a run that isn't your first, will potentially wipe E.G.O. from other runs. There is a special day which require you to work for 30 minutes before doing something incredibly challenging, and losing on that day requires you to redo those 30 minutes. This game asks for a tremendous amount of patience from players, and I do not blame anyone for saying "no" to that demand via mods.

However, the incredible amount of charm and the overall experience was something truly magical. The story made me feel an array of emotions, several upon several unscripted moments in the gameplay were fun and memorable, and oh my god the music. I cannot speak for whether or not the variable difficulty spikes and punishments are going to be worth it at all to you, but if you think you have the patience for this game, I would say that I would recommend this game.
